questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct form of the verb?

options.option_text: Neither of the students was present
Neither of the students were present

questions.explanation: With 'neither of + plural noun', the verb is singular: 'Neither of the students WAS present.' Rule: neither/either as subject takes a singular verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The correct passive voice of 'They are building a new bridge' is:

options.option_text: A new bridge is being built by them
A new bridge is built by them
A new bridge was being built by them
A new bridge has been built by them

questions.explanation: Active: They are building (Present Continuous) → Passive: A new bridge is being built by them. Rule: is/am/are + being + past participle.
questions.subject: English

questions.explanation: Conscientious (governed by conscience). Common errors: confusing -ient and -ience spellings. Related: conscience, conscious, unconscious.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'burn the midnight oil' means:
questions.explanation: Burn the midnight oil: stay up late working or studying (historically using an oil lamp). Example: 'She burned the midnight oil to finish her project before the deadline.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'He is one of those writers who has won many awards.'

options.option_text: 'has' should be 'have' — the antecedent of 'who' is 'writers' (plural), not 'one'

questions.explanation: Rule: 'One of those + plural noun + who/that' takes a PLURAL verb. The relative clause refers to 'writers' (plural), not 'one'. Correct: 'one of those writers who HAVE won many awards.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The correct reported speech for 'She said, I will come tomorrow' is:

options.option_text: She said that she would come the next day
She said that she will come the next day
She said that she would come tomorrow
She said that I would come the next day

questions.explanation: Reported speech rules: 'will' → 'would'; 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'; 'I' → 'she'. Result: She said that she would come the next day.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which preposition correctly completes: 'He is good ___ mathematics'?
questions.explanation: 'Good at' (skill/subject): good at mathematics, good at cooking. 'Good in' is non-standard for subjects. 'Good for' = beneficial for someone/something.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding word (e.g., 'dance a flamingo' instead of 'flamenco')

questions.explanation: Malapropism (from Mrs. Malaprop, Sheridan's character): 'He is the very pineapple of politeness' (should be 'pinnacle'). Common exam vocabulary topic.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: To make something bad less severe or more tolerable; to improve

questions.explanation: Ameliorate (Latin: melior = better): to improve a bad situation. 'Measures to ameliorate poverty' = steps to reduce poverty. Antonym: aggravate, exacerbate.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech in: 'The pen is mightier than the sword.'
questions.explanation: Metaphor: a direct comparison without 'like' or 'as'. Pen = written word/ideas; sword = physical force/military. Simile would say 'like a sword'. This is a metaphor.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The team decided to postpone the match', the word 'postpone' is a/an:

options.option_text: Infinitive (to + verb form) acting as object of 'decided'

questions.explanation: 'To postpone' is an infinitive. 'Decided to postpone' = verb + infinitive as object. Gerund = verb + -ing (postponing the match was decided).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence demonstrates correct subject-verb agreement?

options.option_text: The number of students in the class has increased
The number of students in the class have increased
A number of students in the class has arrived
Both A and C are correct

questions.explanation: 'The number' (specific) takes singular verb. 'A number of' (quantity) takes plural. 'The number of students HAS increased' ✓. 'A number of students HAVE arrived' ✓.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: On the whole; mostly; in general

questions.explanation: By and large: idiom meaning 'on the whole' or 'generally speaking'. Origin: nautical — 'by' (into the wind) and 'large' (downwind) covered all sailing conditions.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which is the correct use of 'affect' vs 'effect'?

options.option_text: The drought affected crop yield; the effect was widespread famine
The drought effected crop yield; the affect was famine
The drought affected crop yield; the affect was famine
The drought effected crop yield; the effect was famine

questions.explanation: Affect = verb (to influence). Effect = noun (result). Exception: 'effect' as verb = to bring about ('effect change'). Exam trap: affect/effect is one of the most tested confusable pairs.
questions.subject: English
